cases.question_text: Does a molecule binding at an allosteric site necessarily inhibit an enzyme? Contrast how an allosteric inhibitor and an allosteric activator affect enzyme shape, substrate binding and enzyme activity.

financial_and_transport.deadline_anchor: normal transport case claim after startup prewarm before listener

response.answer_text: No. Binding at an allosteric site does not necessarily inhibit an enzyme, because allosteric regulators can also be activators. [ev_001] [ev_002] An allosteric inhibitor binds to a location other than the active site and induces a conformational change that reduces the enzyme's affinity for its substrate. [ev_001] This change can reduce enzyme activity because the enzyme no longer effectively catalyzes the conversion of substrate to product. [ev_005] An allosteric activator binds to a location away from the active site and induces a conformational change that increases the affinity of the active site for its substrate. [ev_001] [ev_002] In terms of shape, an allosteric inhibition indirectly induces a conformational change to the active site so that the substrate no longer fits, whereas an allosteric activation modifies the shape of the active site to allow a better fit of the substrate. [ev_002] So the inhibitor lowers substrate binding and activity, while the activator raises substrate binding. [ev_001] [ev_002] [ev_005] Allosteric effectors may increase or decrease enzyme activity depending on the prevailing conditions, so the effect on activity is not fixed by the binding site alone. [ev_006]

response.answer_text: A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has only single bonds between neighboring carbons is saturated, because the textbook defines a saturated fatty acid as one with only single bonds between neighboring carbons in the hydrocarbon chain, so that hydrogen atoms attached to the carbon skeleton are maximized [ev_008] [ev_001]. A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has two carbon-carbon double bonds is unsaturated, since the textbook states that when the hydrocarbon chain contains a double bond the fatty acid is unsaturated [ev_008]; having more than one double bond is described as polyunsaturated [ev_008]. An unsaturated fatty acid does not have to contain exactly one double bond: it may have one or more double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain [ev_002] [ev_008]. Fats are described as a stored form of energy [ev_002], and phospholipids comprise the membrane's matrix [ev_002] [ev_003].

Is a fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has two carbon-carbon double bonds saturated or unsaturated, and must an unsaturated fatty acid contain exactly one double bond? Which lipid class is described as a stored form of energy, and which lipid class forms the cell membrane matrix?

financial_and_transport.deadline_anchor: normal transport case claim after startup prewarm before listener

response.answer_text: A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has only single bonds between neighboring carbons is saturated, because the textbook defines a saturated fatty acid this way and says its hydrogen atoms are maximized [ev_008] [ev_001]. A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has two carbon-carbon double bonds is unsaturated, because unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain [ev_002] [ev_009]. An unsaturated fatty acid does not have to contain exactly one double bond; it may have one or more double bonds, and if there is more than one it is called polyunsaturated [ev_002] [ev_008]. Fats are described as a stored form of energy [ev_002], and phospholipids comprise the membrane's matrix [ev_003].
